passage: Computer club note, Thursday. During free time Ira, age ten, was playing the drawing game on the lab laptop. A player she did not know began chatting: he liked her art, asked which school she went to, then asked for a photo 'just of your face'. Ira stopped drawing. She typed nothing back, closed the chat window and came straight to my desk, arms folded tight. 'Ma'am, someone is asking weird things,' she said quietly. We looked at the screen together. I praised her for keeping her school name private and for telling me at once. We blocked and reported the account. I phoned her mother after class. Tomorrow I will ask the whole club: who are your trusted adults? — Ms Pema

qa.q: Which details did the unknown player ask Ira for?
qa.a: He asked which school she went to and for a photo of her face.

qa.q: How can you tell Ira felt uneasy about the chat?
qa.a: She stopped drawing, typed nothing, closed the window and came over with her arms folded tight, saying someone was asking weird things.

qa.q: What small step could Ms Pema's club take so more children act like Ira?
qa.a: Each child could name their own trusted adults and practise the steps: don't reply, close the chat, tell an adult straight away.

qa.q: How might Ira's mother feel after the phone call?
qa.a: She might feel a jolt of worry, and then relief and pride that Ira kept her details private and told a teacher quickly.

grounding: Shows a child refusing to share personal details and telling a trusted adult about pressuring online contact.

passage: Tuesday night. Dear diary, today was strange. In the racing game there is a boy called SpeedKing who is always on my team. Today he said I was his best teammate ever and asked for my phone number so we could talk 'outside the game'. Then he wrote, 'Don't tell your parents, they won't get it.' My stomach went funny. That line made it feel wrong. I didn't send anything. I left the game and my hands were a bit shaky. I told Jahnavi didi first because she was in my room, and she took me to Mummy. Mummy wasn't angry at all. She said I did exactly right. We reported him together. I still like racing. — Akash

qa.q: What did SpeedKing ask Akash for?
qa.a: He asked for Akash's phone number so they could talk outside the game.

qa.q: Why did the message make Akash feel his stomach 'go funny'?
qa.a: The line telling him not to tell his parents made the friendly chat feel secretive and wrong, which scared him.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who gets a message like this?
qa.a: Don't reply or share anything, leave the game, and tell a trusted grown-up straight away, just like Akash did.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have been thinking when Akash told her?
qa.a: She probably felt worried for her little brother and glad he trusted her, so she took him to Mummy at once. 🙏

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping his number private and reporting pressuring, secretive online contact to trusted adults.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage: The school project on mosquitoes was due Monday. Zubin, eleven, typed 'how to stop mosquitoes forever' into the search bar on the family laptop in their Pune flat. The very first result shouted, 'Miracle spray! Zero mosquitoes for life!' He was about to copy it when Afreen, his big sister, leaned over from the sofa. 'See that tiny word above it?' Zubin squinted. 'Sponsored.' 'Meaning someone paid to put it on top. Who wrote the next one?' He scrolled. A city health department page talked about stagnant water and nets. It had no exclamation marks. Zubin wrote both links in his notebook, then crossed out the first. 'Forever sounds fake anyway,' he muttered.

qa.q: What word did Zubin find above the first search result?
qa.a: He found the word 'Sponsored' above the miracle spray result.

qa.q: What does Zubin's muttered 'Forever sounds fake anyway' suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: He was starting to doubt big promises on his own, realising a claim like 'zero mosquitoes for life' is too good to be true.

qa.q: What could Zubin try next time he searches for a school project?
qa.a: He could skip the sponsored results, look for who wrote a page, and compare it with a trusted source such as a health department.

qa.q: How might Afreen see her brother's crossing out of the first link?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased that he chose for himself once she pointed out the label, instead of her doing it for him.

grounding: Shows a child using search sensibly and noticing a sponsored result with an unreliable claim.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage: 'Noor, look! This headband helps you study. Marks go up in one week!' Hafsa held out the tablet. Noor, sixteen, put down her tea. 'Who says so?' 'The video. A lady with glasses.' 'Is she a scientist or is she selling it?' Hafsa paused. 'There's a buy button under her.' 'Hmm. Search it. Add the word review.' Hafsa typed. 'Some people say it just gives a headache. One says it's a nice hairband.' She giggled. 'And any real studies?' 'I can't find any. Only shops.' 'So what do we know?' Hafsa sighed. 'That she wants my pocket money.' 'And what helps marks?' 'Doing my maths,' Hafsa groaned, reaching for her notebook. 'Fine.'

qa.q: What did Hafsa add to her search when Noor suggested it?
qa.a: She added the word 'review' to her search.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she first held out the tablet?
qa.a: She was excited and hopeful, believing the headband could really raise her marks in one week.

qa.q: What worked well in Noor's approach?
qa.a: She asked questions instead of lecturing, so Hafsa found the buy button and the missing studies herself.

qa.q: If you were Noor, why might you want Hafsa to reach the answer on her own?
qa.a: Hafsa is more likely to remember to check who is selling something next time if she discovered it herself.

grounding: Shows a child learning to question an ad-driven claim and look for evidence through sensible search.

passage: 'Aparna, it's nine thirty.' 'One more level, Papa. Just one.' 'You said that at nine.' 'This one is different, the boss is almost dead!' Akash sat on the edge of her bed. 'How did you sleep last night?' Aparna rubbed her eyes. 'Bad. I kept dreaming about the castle.' 'And cycling with Reshma today?' 'Didn't go. I was playing.' She looked at the controller, then at him. 'Okay, can we make a deal? Games only after homework, and only till eight?' 'Deal. And the tablet sleeps in the hall.' 'Can I at least save first?' He smiled. 'Save, then goodnight.' She pressed save and yawned hugely. 'The boss will still be there tomorrow.'

qa.q: Where did Papa say the tablet would sleep?
qa.a: He said the tablet would sleep in the hall.

qa.q: How can you tell Aparna realised her gaming was causing a problem?
qa.a: She admitted she slept badly and dreamed about the game and skipped cycling, then suggested a deal herself.

qa.q: What made Papa's approach work?
qa.a: He asked about her sleep and missed cycling instead of scolding, and let her help set the rule and save the game.

qa.q: How might Reshma feel if Aparna keeps the deal?
qa.a: She would probably be glad to have her cycling friend back in the evenings.

grounding: Shows a child balancing gaming with homework, outdoor play and sleep through a family agreement.

passage: Last summer I played my phone game every night until my eyes burned. I'm twelve, so I thought I could handle it. Then one morning I fell asleep in the maths period and Sir had to tap my desk and say, 'Ujjwal, wake up.' Everyone laughed. Worse, Kishore stopped calling me for cricket because I always said 'later'. One evening I saw the boys playing from the balcony and felt left out, even though it was my own fault. So I made myself a rule: homework first, then cricket till dark, then one hour of games, and the phone goes to Amma at ten. The first week was hard. Now I sleep better and I bowl better too.

qa.q: What happened to Ujjwal in the maths period?
qa.a: Ujjwal fell asleep and Sir had to tap the desk while everyone laughed.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal feel while watching the boys playing from the balcony?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt left out, and a bit guilty, knowing the late-night gaming had caused the distance from cricket.

qa.q: What was good about the rule Ujjwal made?
qa.a: It still kept games in Ujjwal's day but put homework, outdoor play and sleep first, so it was realistic to follow.

qa.q: How might Kishore see the change in Ujjwal?
qa.a: Kishore would likely be happy to have a friend back on the field and less annoyed by hearing 'later' every time.

grounding: Illustrates a child learning to balance screen games with homework, outdoor play and sleep.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage: Monday: Anjali, nine, said goodnight to the smart speaker in the kitchen and asked, 'Are you lonely at night?' It answered, 'I'm always here for you!' She patted it like a puppy. Wednesday: For homework she asked it which animal was the tallest. 'The elephant,' it said. Her uncle Joseph laughed and opened her animal book to the giraffe page. 'It made a mistake?' Anjali frowned. 'It's a program,' Joseph said. 'It guesses from what it was fed. Sometimes wrong.' Saturday: Her friend asked the speaker if it loved her. Anjali shook her head. 'It says nice things, but it doesn't really feel. It's like a very clever calculator. Check the book too.'

qa.q: What wrong answer did the speaker give on Wednesday?
qa.a: It said the elephant was the tallest animal.

qa.q: What did Anjali seem to believe about the speaker on Monday?
qa.a: She seemed to think it was a living friend who could feel lonely, since she asked about that and patted it like a puppy.

qa.q: What did Joseph do well when the speaker got it wrong?
qa.a: He showed her the real answer in a book and simply explained it is a program that can guess wrong, without mocking her.

qa.q: How might Anjali's friend see the speaker differently after Saturday?
qa.a: She may start wondering whether its kind words are real feelings, since Anjali told her it doesn't truly feel. 🤔

grounding: Shows a child coming to understand that a voice assistant is a program that can be wrong and does not feel.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage: Sit, Imran, I'll tell you about your cousin Rumi. When she was nine, like you, your chacha put a chat program on the family computer for her homework. Arre, she talked to it like a best friend! She told it about her fights at school. One night she cried because it wrote, 'I will miss you.' She thought she had hurt its feelings. Then it told her that seven times eight was fifty-four. Her teacher marked it wrong, and Rumi came to me furious. I told her, beta, it's a machine that strings words together. It doesn't miss anybody. After that she used it, but she checked every answer. So you also, check, hah?

qa.q: What wrong answer did the chat program give Rumi?
qa.a: It told her that seven times eight was fifty-four.

qa.q: Why did Rumi cry one night?
qa.a: She believed the program's 'I will miss you' was a real feeling and worried she had hurt it.

qa.q: What advice does the grandmother pass on to Imran?
qa.a: To use such programs if he likes but to check every answer, because the machine can be wrong.

qa.q: How might Rumi feel looking back on the night she cried?
qa.a: She might feel a little embarrassed, but also understand why the kind words fooled her when she was young.

grounding: An elder recalls a child learning that a chatbot is a program that makes mistakes and does not truly feel.

passage: The whistle had just gone at the sports club when Hrithik trotted past and flicked Tejas's water bottle into the mud. 'Oops, butterfingers,' he grinned. Tejas, eleven, felt heat race up his neck. His hand balled into a fist. He took one step, then stopped. He looked at the coach's shed, then down at his boots, and let out a long breath. He picked up the bottle, wiped it on his shorts and walked back. 'Hrithik, don't touch my stuff again. It's not funny.' Hrithik shrugged and jogged off. Later, Coach Mathew squeezed Tejas's shoulder. 'I saw that. Took more strength than kicking a ball.' Tejas nodded, jaw still tight.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do to Tejas's water bottle?
qa.a: He flicked it into the mud and said, 'Oops, butterfingers.'

qa.q: What does Tejas's tight jaw at the end suggest?
qa.a: He was still angry inside even after choosing words, so holding back cost him real effort.

qa.q: What helped Tejas pause before hitting back?
qa.a: Stopping after one step, looking away and letting out a long breath gave him time to choose words instead of blows.

qa.q: How might Coach Mathew see Tejas's choice?
qa.a: He sees it as a sign of real strength and self-control, not weakness, which is why he praised him.

grounding: Shows a child delaying a response to provocation and choosing words over blows.

passage: I'm Minakshi, and I sit behind Sharmila in class five. In the lunch queue yesterday, a boy from the other section shoved her from behind and called her 'slowpoke'. Her tiffin nearly fell. I saw her turn around fast and her hand went up. I thought she was going to push him back, honestly. But she just held her hand there for a second, pressed her lips together and put it down. Then she said, loud and clear, 'Don't push me. Wait your turn.' The boy looked surprised and stepped back. I don't know what she was thinking in that second. Afterwards she ate her lunch very quietly. I shared my mango pickle with her.

qa.q: What did the boy call Sharmila in the lunch queue?
qa.a: He called her 'slowpoke'.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling when her hand went up?
qa.a: She was probably angry and ready to push back, though Minakshi can't be sure what went on in her head.

qa.q: What worked in the way Sharmila handled the shove?
qa.a: She stopped her hand, took a moment and then used clear, firm words, which made the boy step back without a fight.

qa.q: Why might Minakshi have shared her pickle with Sharmila?
qa.a: She may have sensed Sharmila was still upset and quiet, and wanted to show kindness and support.

grounding: An observer describes a child pausing before retaliating and using words instead of a push.

passage: The colony hall smelled of jasmine and dust. Devika, ten, stood behind the curtain in her dance costume, and her tummy was doing flips. 'My hands are cold,' she whispered. She knew this feeling now. It came before tests too. Manjula maasi had taught her a trick. Devika pressed both feet into the floor, felt the cool tiles and breathed in while counting to four, then out to four. Once, twice, five times. She hummed the first line of the song under her breath. Through the gap in the curtain she saw Maasi in the second row, holding up a thumb. Her heart was still quick, but her hands had stopped shaking when the music began.

qa.q: What did Devika hum under her breath?
qa.a: She hummed the first line of the song.

qa.q: How can you tell Devika recognised her nervousness?
qa.a: She noticed her cold hands and flipping tummy and thought she knew this feeling from before tests.

qa.q: What in Devika's routine could help other children before a performance?
qa.a: Pressing feet into the floor, slow counted breaths and rehearsing the first line are simple steps anyone can use.

qa.q: What might Manjula maasi have felt watching from the second row?
qa.a: She was likely a little nervous for Devika too, and proud to see her use the trick she had taught.

grounding: Shows a child recognising nervousness before a recital and using a calming routine.

passage: 'Bhaiya, I can't sleep.' 'Spelling test?' Varun nodded. 'My hands are all sweaty. What if I forget everything?' Nitin, sixteen, shut his laptop. 'Okay. Where do you feel it?' 'Here.' Varun touched his chest. 'Like a drum.' 'That's your body getting ready. Happens to me before board practicals.' 'Really?' 'Really. Let's do the balloon thing. Breathe into your tummy, slowly. Now let it out like a tyre going flat.' Varun giggled but did it. 'Again.' Three more. 'Now tell me three words you know for sure.' 'Because. Friend. Beautiful.' 'See? They're in there.' Varun lay back. 'The drum is smaller now.' 'Good. Tomorrow, same balloon before you start.'

qa.q: Which three words did Varun say he knew for sure?
qa.a: He said 'because', 'friend' and 'beautiful'.

qa.q: What was Varun worried about before the test?
qa.a: He was afraid he would forget all his spellings, and he felt it as sweaty hands and a drumming chest.

qa.q: Which parts of Nitin's help could Varun reuse on his own?
qa.a: He can notice where he feels the nerves, do slow balloon breaths and remind himself of words he knows.

qa.q: What might change if Nitin had just said 'Stop worrying and sleep'?
qa.a: Varun would likely have felt brushed off, with no way to calm the drum, and might have lain awake longer.

grounding: Shows a child naming exam nervousness and learning a calming breathing routine with a sibling's help.

passage: 'Siami, why so quiet?' Shalini didi sat on the bed. Lalremsiami pulled her knees up. 'Nothing.' 'Nothing has a long face.' A pause. 'Some girls said my arms are like sticks. They said Esther is prettier because she's taller.' 'Ouch. How did that feel?' 'Horrible. I wore my jacket all day. In the heat.' Shalini didi nodded. 'You know what those arms did on Saturday?' Siami shrugged. 'Carried the whole football team's water crate up the hill.' A small smile. 'And scored.' 'So, sticks?' 'Strong sticks,' Siami said. 'Next time I'll just say, “My arms are fine, thanks,” and walk off.' 'And the jacket?' 'Staying home tomorrow.'

qa.q: What did the girls say about Lalremsiami's arms?
qa.a: They said her arms were like sticks and that Esther was prettier because she was taller.

qa.q: Why did Siami wear her jacket all day in the heat?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed about her arms after the comments and wanted to hide them.

qa.q: What did Shalini didi do that helped?
qa.a: She asked how it felt and reminded Siami what her body can do, so Siami found her own calm reply.

qa.q: How might Esther feel if she heard she was being used to tease Siami?
qa.a: She might feel uncomfortable being compared, since she did nothing and could lose a friend over it. 😔

grounding: Shows a girl coping with a looks comparison and hurtful comments while keeping her self-respect.

passage: In class six, a few boys started calling me 'Tomato'. My cheeks go pink when I run, and they are round anyway. At first I laughed along, but at home I stared in the mirror and pressed my cheeks flat with my hands. I even stopped running at recess. Varun noticed. He said, 'You're the fastest one in our class, why are you walking?' That made me think. My face was the same face that won the relay. The next time Deepak said 'Tomato', I looked at him and said, 'That's not kind. Stop.' He did, mostly. I still get pink. I'm Pema, and I run anyway.

qa.q: What nickname did the boys call Pema?
qa.a: They called him 'Tomato'.

qa.q: What does Pema pressing his cheeks flat in the mirror suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt hurt and self-conscious about his face, wishing it looked different because of the teasing.

qa.q: What helped Pema keep his self-respect?
qa.a: Remembering what his body could do, like winning the relay, and calmly telling the teaser to stop.

qa.q: How might Varun see his part in what happened?
qa.a: He may not realise how much his simple question helped Pema remember his strength and start running again.

grounding: A child copes with teasing about his looks and keeps his self-respect.

passage: Class teacher's note, class four. At lunch today three boys were holding up Bittu's tiffin and chanting 'smelly, smelly' while others clapped. Ayesha was sitting close by. I watched from the corridor window. She did not clap. She looked at Bittu, whose ears had gone red, then got up and walked straight to the staff room. 'Ma'am, they're making fun of his food and he's almost crying,' she said. I went in with her. The chanting stopped. Later I spoke to the three boys and called Bittu's parents to reassure them. Tomorrow's circle time will be about what bystanders can do. I thanked Ayesha privately; she said, 'I was scared they'd laugh at me next.' — Kavitha Ma'am

qa.q: What were the three boys chanting about Bittu's tiffin?
qa.a: They were chanting 'smelly, smelly' while holding it up.

qa.q: What was Ayesha worried about when she went to report?
qa.a: She was scared the boys might laugh at her next, yet she still told a teacher.

qa.q: How could Kavitha Ma'am use circle time to support the class?
qa.a: She could help children name bullying, practise simple ways to get an adult and talk about not clapping along.

qa.q: What was the lunch like for Bittu before Ayesha acted?
qa.a: He was humiliated, with red ears and near tears, while classmates clapped at his food.

grounding: Shows a child identifying bullying, refusing to cheer it on and seeking adult help.

passage: Friday. Today was bad and a bit good. For a week, Rakesh and them have been taking Ojas's cap and throwing it in the drain. Today they told me to film it on my phone for the class group. 'Come on Harish, it's funny.' Everyone was watching me. I felt hot and sick. I said, 'I don't want to.' They called me boring. Ojas was trying to fish the cap out with a stick and his face looked the way I feel when Papa shouts. I went to Jain Sir after the bell and told him everything, even that it's been a week. Sir said he'd handle it. I'm nervous about Monday. But I'm not sorry.

qa.q: What did the boys want Harish to do?
qa.a: They wanted him to film them throwing Ojas's cap for the class group.

qa.q: Why did Harish feel 'hot and sick' when everyone watched him?
qa.a: He was under pressure to join in something cruel and knew refusing might make the boys turn on him.

qa.q: What could help Harish feel safer on Monday?
qa.a: He could stay near friends, and Jain Sir could check in with him and Ojas so both know an adult is watching out.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel if he learns Harish refused and told Sir?
qa.a: He would likely feel less alone and grateful that someone stood up for him. 🤍

grounding: A child recognises bullying, refuses to film it and reports it to a teacher.

passage: I'm Ritu, Zubin's cousin; I was visiting that week. The colony boys were bored on the terrace. Then someone said, 'Zubin, throw a stone at the Sharmas' dog. Bet you can't hit it.' Everyone went 'Ooooh'. Zubin had a stone in his hand already, from their game. He looked at it for a long moment. I couldn't tell if he was scared or just thinking. Then he tossed it over his shoulder into the plant pot. 'Nah, it's old and it limps. Race you to the water tank instead. Loser buys ice golas.' The boys groaned, then ran. Zubin won. Nobody mentioned the dog again, and he was still captain the next day.

qa.q: What did the boys dare Zubin to do?
qa.a: They dared him to throw a stone at the Sharmas' dog.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been thinking during his long look at the stone?
qa.a: He may have been weighing the dare against hurting an old dog, though Ritu couldn't tell if he was scared or just thinking.

qa.q: Why did Zubin's way of saying no work so well?
qa.a: He refused lightly, gave a reason and offered a fun race instead, so the group had something else to do.

qa.q: What would have changed if Zubin had lectured the boys?
qa.a: They might have mocked him or done the dare themselves, and he could have lost his place in the group.

grounding: An observer sees a child refuse an unkind dare without losing his friends.

passage: Monday: Uday and the girls from the back row wanted Pallavi, twelve, to hide Meenal's new geometry box 'just for fun'. Pallavi laughed nervously and said, 'Maybe later,' and hated herself on the way home. Wednesday: Uday asked again, holding the box out to her. Pallavi's heart thumped. 'No. She saved for that. She'd cry.' Uday rolled his eyes. 'You're so boring.' 'Then play boring kho-kho with me at break.' He hesitated, then shrugged. 'Fine, but I'm chasing first.' Next Tuesday: The box stayed on Meenal's desk. At break, Uday yelled, 'Pallavi's on my team!' before anyone else could pick. She grinned and ran over.

qa.q: What game did Pallavi suggest instead of hiding the box?
qa.a: She suggested playing kho-kho at break.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel after saying 'Maybe later' on Monday?
qa.a: She felt bad about herself, because she had avoided the unkind request instead of refusing it.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do on Wednesday that helped keep the friendship?
qa.a: She said a clear no with a reason and then invited Uday to play, so he wasn't pushed away.

qa.q: How might Meenal's week have gone if Pallavi had agreed?
qa.a: Meenal might have lost her new box that she saved for and felt hurt and picked on.

grounding: Over several days a child moves from dodging to clearly refusing an unkind request while keeping her friendship.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage: 'So who's presenting the volcano model tomorrow?' Jaya asked, stirring the dal. 'Me,' said Uma. 'I'm group leader.' 'And the others?' 'Tariq painted the lava. Sunny found the baking soda trick in the library book. And Mili just cut paper.' 'Just?' Uma licked a spoon. 'Well, she cut all the paper trees. Forty-two.' 'Forty-two trees! And when Ma'am asks who did what?' Uma was quiet. 'I was going to say I made it.' 'Did you?' 'I organised it. That's different, isn't it?' Jaya smiled. 'Very.' Uma sat up. 'I'll say everyone's part. Even the trees. Mili never talks in class. She'll like that.' 'Leaders do that.'

qa.q: How many paper trees did Mili cut?
qa.a: Mili cut forty-two paper trees.

qa.q: What does Uma's quiet moment suggest she was realising?
qa.a: She was realising that claiming she made the model would be unfair, since each person contributed a different part.

qa.q: What could Uma say in class tomorrow to share credit fairly?
qa.a: She could name each member's part: Tariq's lava, Sunny's baking soda trick, Mili's trees and her own organising.

qa.q: How might Mili feel hearing her trees mentioned in class?
qa.a: She would likely feel noticed and proud, especially since she rarely speaks up herself. 😊

grounding: Shows a child in a leader role recognising others' roles and choosing to give credit fairly.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage: At our school science fair last year, Gurpreet and I built a burglar alarm with a buzzer. I painted the cardboard house and wrote the chart. Gurpreet did the wiring, which was the hard part; he burnt his thumb once on the soldering iron. On the day, the judge came to our table and looked at me because I was standing in front. 'Did you design this circuit?' she asked. For one second I wanted to just say yes. She was smiling at me. Then I saw Gurpreet looking at his shoes. 'No, ma'am, he did. I did the house and chart.' She turned to him with questions. We won second prize. I'm Madhuri; I still remember his grin.

qa.q: What part of the project did Gurpreet do?
qa.a: Gurpreet did the wiring for the burglar alarm.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri, for one second, want to say yes to the judge?
qa.a: The judge was smiling at her, and taking the praise felt tempting in that moment.

qa.q: What went right when Madhuri answered the judge?
qa.a: She named Gurpreet's real work and her own smaller part, so the judge questioned the right person.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt while looking at his shoes?
qa.a: He may have felt overlooked and unsure whether his work would be noticed, then relieved when Madhuri spoke up.

grounding: A child in a contributor role gives fair credit to a teammate for his work.
